Amplitude estimation turns a flag’s probability into a coherent circuit’s rotation angle. Instead of observing the flag repeatedly, the fundamental algorithm applies controlled amplification steps and estimates their eigenphases 

Brassard et al., 2002. This is useful when sample preparation or predicate evaluation is expensive and coherent access and inverse access are available. Those operations are explicit parts of the circuit here.

Implemented scope

Standard phase-estimation amplitude estimation, preparation/inverse preparation, a threshold predicate, both reflections, complete controlled powers, final measurements, and an ideal median-confidence contract are implemented. Bounded circuits and their primitive lowering are checked against independent analytic distributions; a separately labeled classical categorical experiment checks median coverage.

The resource section contains a conditional mean-fit surface-code projection. There is no generated Clifford+T synthesis certificate or hardware amplitude-confidence guarantee. Iterative confidence-interval amplitude estimation, a practical application predicate and formal Lean coverage remain planned.

Given a preparation circuitA|0\rangle=\sqrt{1-a}|\psi_0\rangle|0\rangle+
\sqrt a|\psi_1\rangle|1\rangle,

estimate a with a stated absolute error and confidence. Write a=\sin^2\theta. Reflection about the prepared state followed by reflection of the good subspace rotates their two-dimensional span by 2\theta. Its two eigenphases are \pm\theta/\pi in units of a full turn. Both decode to the same probability through \sin^2(\pi\phi).

Our classical input is an n-bit uniform register and threshold k; the reversible flag predicate is [x<k]. The independent answer is a=k/2^n. Because that threshold probability is already known, this is an implementation/accounting example with no application advantage. A practical integration, finance or counting problem needs its own reversible predicate and loading cost.

The comparator toggles the flag when the first bit differing from the threshold is zero and the threshold bit is one. At most n disjoint prefix terms use X and multi-controlled-X, preserving all data bits with no work register or enumerated truth table. q[0] is the least significant data bit; q[n] is the flag.

Let S_0=I-2|0\rangle\langle0| and S_g=I-2\Pi_g. Our iterate isQ=-A S_0 A^\dagger S_g.

Chronologically it applies S_g,A^\dagger,S_0,A, and a global minus sign. That sign matters once Q is controlled. Dropping it shifts the estimated phase and gives a wrong amplitude; the a=1 test catches this error. S_0 is actual X/MCZ/X, with MCZ lowered through H/MCX/H; S_g is Z on the flag.

Prepare A|0\rangle, add m phase qubits in |+\rangle, apply controlled Q^{2^j} from wire j, then inverse QFT and phase measurement. Each power is actual repeated Q access, rather than an opaque matrix. For M=2^m, output y decodes as\widehat a(y)=\sin^2(\pi y/M).

The default uses two data qubits, threshold one, a flag and four phase qubits: seven logical qubits, a=1/4, one initial preparation and 15 controlled iterates.

preparation = threshold_preparation(n_data, threshold)
preparation.draw(output="mpl", fold=40, scale=.9)



measured = build_amplitude_estimation(n_data, threshold, phase_bits, measure=True)
measured.draw(output="mpl", fold=45, scale=.6)



The phase law is the equal mixture of independent geometric-sum QPE laws at \phi=1/6 and 5/6. Peaks y=3,13 each have probability about 0.344269 and decode to 0.308658284, an error about 0.0586583. The mean over all decoded outcomes is 0.296875; this coarse estimator is not unbiased.

BHMT Theorem 12 gives single-run success at least p_0=8/\pi^2 for|\widehat a-a|\le 2\pi\sqrt{a(1-a)}/M+\pi^2/M^2.

Our answer-independent contract uses \epsilon_M=\min(1,\pi/M+\pi^2/M^2). At m=4 it is 0.234902683, so the example deliberately has coarse precision. The bound can be conservative or trivial at very small m.

Run the complete circuit independently an odd number R of times and take the median of decoded outcomes. If a majority lies in the interval, its median does too. A binomial majority-tail bound is\sum_{j=(R+1)/2}^{R}{R\choose j}(1-p_0)^j p_0^{R-j}.

Requested ideal failure 0.005 needs R=15 under this bound; the value is about 0.00296846. The generator also computes the exact ideal interval-failure probability for this discrete distribution and checks 10,000 classical categorical ensembles at seed 8127. These draw from the exact ideal law; physical circuits are not run.

Classical Bernoulli sampling of the same preparation and flag needs N\ge\log(2/\delta)/(2\epsilon_M^2) shots by Hoeffding. At equal \epsilon_M and \delta=0.005, this is 55 preparations/readouts. The quantum proposal uses 15 full QPE runs including 465 predicate or inverse-predicate calls. Query complexity does not imply a lower compiled cost here, and the known threshold already gives an exact classical shortcut.

For constant success probability, standard amplitude estimation needs O(1/\epsilon) amplification queries and O(n+\log(1/\epsilon)) live qubits. This independent median multiplies work by O(\log(1/\delta)). The QFT costs O(m^2) controlled phases. Each query contains preparation, its inverse and both reflections. Its primitive cost depends on the comparator controls and pinned compiler; the compiled ledger assigns no oracle unit cost.

Grover search amplifies the probability of a marked item using a reversible predicate and a reflection about a uniform superposition 

Grover, 1996. It is a useful first implementation because its circuit is small enough to inspect and its ideal success probability has a closed form. The survey gives the broader application and end-to-end complexity context 

Dalzell et al., 2025.

Note

Implementation status

The three-qubit demo is simulated and checked against the mathematical prediction during the site build. The generator supports other sizes. The exported circuit includes the oracle and diffuser decomposed into gates; the fixed three-qubit circuit compiles to exact Clifford and T operations, while larger circuits can require arbitrary-angle synthesis. The 

in-page surface-code baseline records the physical assumptions and estimator output.

There are N=2^n computational basis states and exactly one marked state m. The phase oracle applies -1 to \lvert m\rangle and leaves every other basis state unchanged. Our explicit oracle compares the register to a known integer using X gates and a multi-controlled phase flip. This is a teaching example: knowing the target already solves the classical problem. A practical search application must replace it with a reversible problem predicate and count that predicate’s construction, evaluation, and uncomputation.

The notebook uses Qiskit core, an open-source circuit library released under Apache 2.0. The circuit generator is an original implementation using Qiskit core. See the 

upstream repository and the 

downloadable implementation source.

Prepare the uniform state with H^{\otimes n}. Repeat the phase oracle followed by reflection about that uniform state, then measure and verify the candidate. The two reflections rotate the state toward the marked subspace: the phase flip changes relative signs, and the diffuser converts that sign change into increased marked-state amplitude.

For one marked item among N=2^n, the first success peak uses \Theta(\sqrt N) oracle calls 

Grover, 1996. Register width n and candidate count N are different size parameters. An oracle call is not a fixed gate cost: if its actual reversible construction costs C_O(n) and diffusion costs C_D(n), one trial costs preparation plus r[C_O(n)+C_D(n)] and readout. The equality oracle below has its own explicit decomposition; an application predicate requires a separate ledger.

Amplitude amplification generalizes the uniform input to a specified preparation circuit and success predicate. Its preparation inverse and reflections must be implemented and counted. This page implements the single-target Grover case; 

oblivious amplification in dynamics is a separate construction and task.

We prepare three qubits in the uniform superposition, mark integer 5 (bitstring 101), and apply two Grover iterations. Qiskit displays bitstrings with the most significant bit first; circuit wire q[0] represents the least significant bit.

The circuit below is reused directly from the saved output of the executable notebook.

n_qubits, marked = 3, 5
iterations = optimal_iterations(n_qubits)

Let \theta=\arcsin(1/\sqrt{N}). After r iterations, the ideal probability of the marked state isP(m)=\sin^2((2r+1)\theta).

For N=8 and r=2, this is 0.9453125. The exact statevector simulation checks this value. Sampling a real device would additionally introduce shot noise and device errors.

These logical counts are not physical qubit counts. A fault-tolerant estimate must specify rotation precision, logical error budget, code distance, state-distillation factories, timing, and failure probability. The

The scaling CSV covers 2–8 qubits with the all-ones target. It contains decomposed circuit counts rather than simulated large-register results. Changing the target changes which X gates are needed, and compilation choices can change gate counts.

The first baseline estimates the circuit from this chapter: initialization, the explicit equality predicate, diffusion, and final measurements. It uses the open-source

These results describe an illustrative hardware model. They do not establish an application speedup or a measured hardware performance guarantee. The equality oracle tests a known three-bit string; an application predicate or database access would need its own implementation and cost.

The

Physical space/time depends additionally on synthesis precision, code distances, factory allocation and scheduling. Report peak physical qubits Q_{\rm peak}, serial runtime T and their product Q_{\rm peak}T as a rectangular space-time proxy; the product is not the integral of occupancy over time.

For the default example, one state is marked among eight and two Grover iterations are used. The ideal success probability per circuit execution isp_{\mathrm{success}} = \sin^2\!\left(5\arcsin(1/\sqrt{8})\right) = 0.9453125.

We set an overall failure target of 1%, reserve 0.5% for sampling failure and 0.5% for physical faults, and run two trials serially. Ideal sampling failure is (1-p_{\mathrm{success}})^2\approx0.002991. Each trial receives a physical-failure allowance of 0.25%. A union bound gives overall failure at most 0.7991% under the declared model and ideal verification assumptions. The report records the tighter bound from each returned estimate.

Peak physical qubits remain the per-trial peak because trials run serially. Runtime is multiplied by two. This chapter implements a small dynamics task with original gate construction and an independent classical answer. It belongs to the 

quantum-simulation umbrella; 

open systems and 

Gibbs preparation have separate tracks.

Implementation status

First- and second-order product formulas implement dynamics with state, operator and observable checks. Taylor LCU has actual PREPARE/SELECT, uncomputation and a measured/reset postselection schedule. Qubitization access, a standalone degree-14 QSP cosine filter, complex postselected evolution and a separate integer-round oblivious-amplification path are checked. Deterministic evolution remains planned. Physical estimates remain with the shared resource integration. No hardware advantage or formal proof is claimed.

Use three spins on an open chain withH=A+B,\quad A=Z_0Z_1+Z_1Z_2,\quad B=0.7(X_0+X_1+X_2).

The coupling J=1 defines the energy unit, \hbar=1, and time is t=1 in inverse coupling units. Prepare |\psi_0\rangle=|000\rangle. The state task approximates U(t)|\psi_0\rangle for U(t)=e^{-iHt}; the observable task estimates \langle Z_0\rangle after evolution. These outputs have different repetition costs. The exact small classical observable is approximately 0.404255857287.

The input is an explicit Pauli coefficient list. Qiskit labels read q[2] q[1] q[0]: the terms are IZZ, ZZI, IIX, IXI, XII. The observable assigns +1 to bit 0 equal to zero and -1 to bit 0 equal to one. The zero basis input needs no preparation gates; a device still needs initialization. No external data loading is modeled.

For an approximation V, report spectral operator error \|V-U\|_2, state-vector error \|V\psi_0-U\psi_0\|_2, state infidelity and observable bias separately. Vector error retains phase; infidelity does not. For normalized states, a state-vector error \epsilon bounds this observable bias by 2\epsilon.

The Hamiltonian terms are easy to exponentiate individually even when their sum is not. Product formulas alternate those simple rotations. Shorter steps reduce the mismatch caused by noncommutation; a symmetric schedule cancels the leading splitting error. The fixed example below makes that error visible against exact small-system evolution.

Let \delta=t/r. Applying an A layer followed chronologically by a B layer givesV_1(t;r)=\left(e^{-iB\delta}e^{-iA\delta}\right)^r.

Linear systems occur in differential equations, regression and optimization. A quantum linear-system algorithm prepares a state proportional to A^{-1}b and extracts a useful observable. This can be attractive when a matrix has economical quantum access and the downstream task needs a few expectations rather than the entire vector. Loading an arbitrary matrix or reading every solution entry can remove that attraction. The survey’s end-to-end perspective makes access and output assumptions central 

Dalzell et al., 2025.

The intuition is spectral: in an eigenbasis of A, divide each amplitude of b by its eigenvalue. HHL stores the eigenvalue in a clock, uses it to control a flag rotation, then erases the clock 

Harrow et al., 2009. QSVT instead applies a polynomial to a block encoding of A, avoiding the eigenvalue register 

Gilyén et al., 2019. Both need normalization, a success procedure and readout.

No certified synthesis or conditional-output guarantee is provided. The QDK mean fit is a cost model. Clean initialization timing/faults, classical preprocessing/compilation/readout and concrete synthesis are excluded. The main page states the separate norm certificate postselection would require. Actual accepted branches are compared with (5B-4B^3)b/4 and a normalized classical solve on the stated spectrum. Tests include X, Y and multi-qubit words, real/complex preparation, X/Y/Z basis changes, recursive rejection of hidden nonunitary preparation, lowering and deterministic phase reproduction. A generic-spectrum test detects that the cubic is not an inverse. Independent review checked 15 Hermitian Pauli sums against independent Kronecker matrices.

Dense checks allow six data/12 total wires; generated circuits are separately bounded. No Lean or other integrated formal proof covers this circuit. The 

notebook and 

public package supply the original implementation, shared Pauli/QSP dependencies and tests. Run python scripts/generate_linear_systems_qsvt.py with --word to specify actual access. Versions, licenses and primary sources are recorded on the main page and artifacts.

Farhi et al., 2014

Peruzzo et al., 2014. Both are hybrid workflows: classical parameter search and repeated state preparations needed to evaluate an objective belong to the algorithm. Here we make those operations inspectable on two small problems.

The first resource record contains logical circuit inputs and the complete demonstrated workload. Arbitrary rotations remain unsynthesized. The finite-shot increment adds conditional physical projections of a fixed final readout. The 

recorded-trajectory replay maps all stored training and holdout circuits, while the 

portability cases test changed inputs with fixed starts. Predictive physical estimates of a fresh hardware-driven adaptive optimization remain planned.

hierarchy.lvl2: QAOA: MaxCut on a four-vertex cycle
QAOA: MaxCut on a four-vertex cycle

records.content:
Number the vertices 0,1,2,3 and supply the edge list\mathcal E=\{(0,1),(1,2),(2,3),(0,3)\}.

For an assignment z=(z_0,z_1,z_2,z_3), the cut size and cost operator areC(z)=\sum_{(u,v)\in\mathcal E}[z_u\ne z_v],\qquad
C=\sum_{(u,v)\in\mathcal E}\frac{I-Z_uZ_v}{2}.

The classical maximum is four, attained by the two alternating assignments. Qiskit wire q[0] is the least significant bit, so displayed strings read z_3z_2z_1z_0; the optimal strings are 0101 and 1010. Enumeration evaluates the edge predicate directly rather than consulting the quantum objective routine.

Starting from |+\rangle^{\otimes4}, one QAOA layer applies|\psi(\gamma,\beta)\rangle=
e^{-i\beta\sum_j X_j}e^{-i\gamma C}|+\rangle^{\otimes4}.

The optimizer minimizes f(\gamma,\beta)=-\langle C\rangle. Angles are radians. Our gate convention is R_P(\alpha)=e^{-i\alpha P/2}: the mixer uses rx(2*beta) on every vertex. For each edge, the phase circuit is cx(u,v); rz(-gamma,v); cx(u,v). This realizes e^{+i\gamma Z_uZ_v/2}; the omitted identity contribution changes only the global phase. There is no dense-matrix oracle or unexplained access operation.



For this cycle and one layer, an independent expression for the expected cut is\langle C\rangle=2+\sin(4\beta)\sin(2\gamma).

Thus \gamma=\pi/4, \beta=\pi/8 gives mean cut three, compared with the classical maximum four. The ratio 3/4 describes an expected cut on this instance. It does not mean every draw has cut three. At these analytic angles, the probabilities of cut sizes zero, two, and four are 1/32, 14/32, and 17/32. Each maximum-cut bitstring has probability 17/64. The saved plot and run record report the corresponding numerical distribution for the fitted angles.





All edges are diagonal in the computational basis. One all-Z measurement produces an assignment and evaluates all four edge contributions together. For a fixed optimized state with best-cut probability p_\star, N independent ideal draws contain a maximum cut with probability 1-(1-p_\star)^N. At the analytic angles, seven draws give success above 0.99. This calculation assumes ideal preparations at those fixed angles and independent draws; it does not predict optimizer success or noisy-device performance.

Use dimensionless coefficients and the HamiltonianH=-Z_0-Z_1+\frac12 X_0X_1.

In basis order |q_1q_0\rangle=|00\rangle,|01\rangle,|10\rangle,|11\rangle, its matrix isH=\begin{pmatrix}
-2&0&0&1/2\\
0&0&1/2&0\\
0&1/2&0&0\\
1/2&0&0&2
\end{pmatrix}.

Its eigenvalues are -\sqrt{17}/2,-1/2,1/2,\sqrt{17}/2, so the reference ground energy is E_0=-\sqrt{17}/2\approx-2.061552813. This is a stated teaching Hamiltonian, rather than a molecule or chemistry workload with uncounted integral preparation.

Prepare |00\rangle, apply ry(theta,0), and then cx(0,1). The resulting state is|\psi(\theta)\rangle=
\cos(\theta/2)|00\rangle+\sin(\theta/2)|11\rangle.



The independent scalar expectation isE(\theta)=-2\cos\theta+\frac12\sin\theta.

Its minimum is the full matrix ground energy, attained at \theta=-\arctan(1/4) modulo 2\pi. This ansatz can represent the exact ground state of this particular Hamiltonian. The generator and notebook compare the circuit expectation, matrix eigenvalue, and scalar formula; this expressibility statement does not extend to a general Hamiltonian or ansatz.



Finite-shot energy evaluation uses two groups. In the all-Z group, one bitstring yields the joint value -Z_0-Z_1; its sample variance includes covariance of the Z terms. In the all-X group, apply H to both qubits before computational-basis measurement and score \tfrac12X_0X_1. Adding the group means estimates total energy. The measurement protocol requires a fresh ansatz preparation for each shot, and H basis changes and final measurements appear in the exports. The implementation obtains each group’s statevector probabilities and draws its counts classically. Shot noise can put a sampled energy below E_0 even though the exact expectation obeys the variational bound.

The original optimizer is a small coordinate polling routine. It evaluates the initial point, then every negative and positive coordinate displacement in a fixed order. If the best candidate reduces the minimized objective by more than 

10-12, it accepts that candidate; otherwise it halves the step. The initial step is 0.4 radians. It stops when the step falls below 

10-6 radians or after 128 sweeps, and records which condition stopped each run. Coordinates are wrapped modulo 2\pi.

QAOA initial points are (\gamma,\beta)=(0.2,0.1),(0.6,0.4),(-0.3,0.25). VQE initial angles are 0.6,-1.1,2.2. Every optimization objective uses an exact ideal statevector, with zero measurement shots. The run record retains accepted points, rejected candidates, iterations, evaluation counts, parameters, elapsed objective time, and total classical optimization time. Wall-clock timings include the classical simulator and are machine-dependent; they are not hardware execution times.



The primary fitted angles are then evaluated in separate ideal finite-shot experiments with seeds 7, 19, and 41, using 2,048 shots per measurement group per seed. Samples are drawn classically from statevector probabilities; repeated physical circuits are not executed. These first-increment experiments do not feed sampled objectives back to the optimizer. They report counts, sampled objectives, exact expectations, sample standard errors, and achieved output quality. Changing initialization probes optimization variability; changing the sampling seed probes readout variability. The 

next increment records an actual sampled parameter search with fresh final validation. Both increments use ideal simulation and exclude device noise and error mitigation.

QAOA uses one all-Z group. Each bitstring yields its complete cut size C(z), sharing the outcomes across all four edges. The minimized estimate is \widehat f_Q=-\overline C. Its descriptive standard error is s_Q=\sqrt{\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(C)/N}, using sample variance of whole cut scores.

+\frac{\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(Y_X)}{N_X}}.

The two Z terms are scored jointly from the same bitstrings, so their covariance is retained. They are not treated as independent term measurements. Exhaustive enumeration of its eight assignments gives cut values [0,2,2,2,2,2,2,0] in integer bitstring order. The classical maximum is two. In basis order |q_1q_0\rangle=|00\rangle,|01\rangle,|10\rangle,|11\rangle,H_2=\begin{pmatrix}
-1.4&0&0&0.4\\
0&0.2&0.4&0\\
0&0.4&-0.2&0\\
0.4&0&0&1.4
\end{pmatrix}.

Its independent energy formula isE_2(\theta)=-1.4\cos\theta+0.4\sin\theta.

This has its minimum at \theta=-\arctan(2/7) modulo 2\pi, equal to the matrix ground energy. Thus this second Hamiltonian still has a ground state in the same even-parity ansatz family. Many quantum tasks encode the answer in an eigenphase: an energy in Hamiltonian evolution, an order in modular arithmetic, or a probability in amplitude amplification. A phase is not directly visible in a computational-basis measurement. Phase estimation uses controlled evolution and interference to turn it into a classical binary record 

Cleve et al., 1998.

The quantum Fourier transform (QFT) combines the phases carried by a register. Phase estimation first prepares a superposition of different evolution lengths, then applies an inverse QFT so that matching phases add and mismatching phases cancel. QFT produces a quantum state; it does not return every entry of a classical Fourier transform in one measurement. This chapter supplies reusable components for the survey’s applications 

Dalzell et al., 2025.

Implemented scope

Exact and truncated QFT, textbook QPE and one-ancilla feedback QPE have explicit circuits and independent small-instance checks. Five static-QPE surface-code projections are computed under the audited conditional mean-fit model. Eigenstate preparation for an arbitrary application and certified rotation synthesis remain application responsibilities. No integrated Lean proof is supplied.

For N=2^m, our positive-sign QFT convention isF_N\lvert x\rangle=\frac{1}{\sqrt N}\sum_{y=0}^{N-1}e^{2\pi ixy/N}\lvert y\rangle.

The circuit uses m Hadamards, m(m-1)/2 controlled-phase gates and \lfloor m/2\rfloor swaps. Wire q[0] is the least-significant bit. Swaps are included, so the matrix is the expression above rather than a bit-reversed variant. The inverse reverses the gate order and the phase signs.

QPE accepts an explicit n-qubit circuit U and an explicit preparation circuit for an eigenstateU\lvert\psi\rangle=e^{2\pi i\phi}\lvert\psi\rangle,\qquad 0\leq\phi<1.

It prepares m phase qubits with Hadamards, applies controlled U^{2^j} from phase wire j, applies F_N^\dagger and measures those m wires. The decoded integer y estimates \phi by y/N. Our generator constructs each power from 2^j complete controlled calls to the supplied U; no power or dense matrix is treated as a free oracle. A supplied global phase becomes a conditional phase and is retained.

For an eigenstate, the independent reference distribution isP(y)=\frac{1}{N^2}\left|\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}e^{2\pi ik(\phi-y/N)}\right|^2.

A phase exactly on the grid is recovered with ideal probability one. For other phases, the two adjacent grid points are within circular error 1/N and together have probability at least 8/\pi^2. The median of 15 independent scalar estimates has majority-failure bound below 0.005 at that single-run bound. Scalar medians require \phi\in[1/N,1-1/N], so the good interval does not cross the phase branch cut. A circular median is not implemented. If the input is a superposition of eigenstates, the output is the corresponding phase mixture; a good phase-resolution bound does not establish overlap with the desired eigenstate.

Approximate QFT omits small controlled rotations and includes a derived spectral-norm omission bound. It changes circuit approximation and must share the application’s coherent error allowance.

Iterative feedback QPE reuses one phase ancilla, measures least-significant output bits first and applies actual classical feedback. It has a separate circuit, notebook and bounded ideal instrument check.

Alternative phase-inference procedures, noisy experimental robustness and application-specific fast controlled powers remain planned. Their confidence and access costs are not inferred from these demos.

The four-wire QFT below comes from the executed notebook. Its matrix is compared directly with the mathematical definition.

plt.close("all")



The QPE demo uses U=P(2\pi\times0.3) and prepares \lvert1\rangle with X. The phase is already known to the constructor, making this a transparent correctness example. It is not an energy or factoring benchmark. With m=5, the six-wire circuit applies 31 controlled U calls.

Fifteen seeded ideal draws give median 10/32=0.3125, within 1/32 of 0.3. The draws use validated ideal circuit probabilities; they are not hardware executions.

An exact m-wire Fourier circuit has quadratic controlled-phase count. Its longest-range phases are exponentially small. Omitting those phases reduces gate construction and eventual synthesis work at a declared coherent approximation cost, following the approximate-transform idea of Coppersmith 

Coppersmith, 1994.

build_qft(m, max_distance=b) retains the Hadamards and final swaps, and keeps only controlled phases with wire separation d\leq b. A retained gate has angle \pi/2^d. The retained count is \sum_{d=1}^{b}(m-d), giving O(mb) controlled phases rather than O(m^2). Setting b=m-1 is the exact circuit; b=0 retains only Hadamards and swaps.

For an omitted phase \theta, \|CP(\theta)-I\|_2=2|\sin(\theta/2)|\leq|\theta|. A telescoping product of unitary gates therefore gives the original bound\|\widetilde F_N-F_N\|_2\leq
\min\!\left(2,\sum_{d=b+1}^{m-1}(m-d)\frac{\pi}{2^d}\right)
\leq\min(2,\pi m/2^b).

The inverse has the same bound. Choosing b\geq\lceil\log_2(\pi m/\eta)\rceil, capped at m-1, meets a sufficient spectral-norm omission allowance \eta. This bound covers the omitted ideal phases. It does not cover inaccuracies in retained rotations, physical faults or application readout confidence.

The 

generated table compares explicit source circuits. At m=32, cutoff b=14 retains 343 controlled phases instead of 496, with telescoping bound about 0.003067963. These larger circuits were generated and counted, not densely simulated. Logical count reduction alone does not establish physical improvement: retained rotation synthesis and factory scheduling must be compared under the same application and accuracy contract.

       "telescoping_bound": bound, "controlled_phases": int(approx.count_ops()["cp"])})

The phase register can be measured one bit at a time when its inverse Fourier transform is immediately followed by readout. Earlier outcomes then select later single-qubit corrections, replacing coherent Fourier interactions with classical feedback 

Griffiths & Niu, 1996.

Our explicit circuit uses n+1 quantum wires and m classical output bits. In round r=0,\ldots,m-1 it resets the phase ancilla, applies H and 2^{m-r-1} controlled calls to U, applies corrections selected by previous recorded bits, applies H and measures into c[r]. A previous c[l]=1 triggersP\!\left(-\frac{2\pi}{2^{r-l+1}}\right),\qquad l<r.

The least-significant output bit is obtained first. Displaying c[m-1]...c[0] gives the usual binary integer y and phase y/2^m. The eigenstate is prepared once and retained between rounds in the ideal instrument. For a superposition of eigenstates, the retained system and record become correlated; the checked final phase distribution is the expected mixture.

instrument = build_iterative_qpe(m, u, prep)

np.testing.assert_allclose(feedback, conventional, atol=3e-13, rtol=0)

       "feedback_reference_max_error": float(np.max(abs(feedback-reference))),
       "feedback_static_max_error": float(np.max(abs(feedback-conventional))),
       "method": "actual ideal instrument branch enumeration"})



The default is U=P(2\pi\times0.3), prepared \lvert1\rangle, and five output bits. The actual if_else, measurement and reset instrument is evaluated by bounded branch enumeration: project the measured wire, weight each outcome, apply its selected correction and continue. It is not replaced by the known-phase distribution formula. The result matches conventional QPE and the independent Dirichlet reference within 2.4\times10^{-15}.

The quantum width falls from n+m to n+1 while retaining m classical bits. Each complete execution still applies 2^m-1 controlled U calls, 2m H gates, m reset instructions, m measurements and up to m(m-1)/2 selected correction gates. Fifteen independent runs of the default use 465 controlled calls, 75 measurements and 75 resets, with fresh preparation for each run.

The source ledger separates unconditional primitive operations from conditional blocks. A conditional gate is charged on the corresponding branch; recording a worst-case branch bound does not produce an average latency model. The executed circuit includes reset even though an ideal measured eigenstate can allow equivalent feedback initialization strategies. Reset faults and classical feed-forward delays are not silently omitted.

Physical resources remain pending for this dynamic circuit. The shared static QDK adapter rejects intermediate measurement, reset and feedback. The parent chapter’s static-QPE numbers do not cover this implementation and cannot establish that ancilla savings lower physical cost. Each example fixes the physical model, input, units, requested output and measurement protocol. Hamiltonian dynamics uses an open noncommuting spin chain. Open-system dynamics includes absorbing decay and a driven-qubit Lindblad splitting. Thermal preparation separates exhaustive diagonal coefficient loading from a Bell-input filter for a noncommuting Pauli Hamiltonian. These are different tasks and are not an equal-task resource comparison.

The dense classical answers check actual gate/dilation/preparation circuits; they are not quantum algorithm implementations. Parameterized generators and simulators have separate limits. purification and its circuit for a thermal mixed state. Important methods have their own pages:

Evidence policy

Factoring an integer becomes easier if we know the period of its modular powers. Shor’s algorithm uses interference to reveal that period: a superposition of exponents is entangled with a^x\bmod N, and an inverse Fourier transform makes samples concentrate near multiples of the reciprocal order 

Shor, 1997. The classical gcd step turns suitable periods into factors. The survey discusses the application and its full resource context 

Dalzell et al., 2025.

Implementation status

The N=15 and N=21 examples execute actual modular-add and modular-multiply circuits, with numerical checks against independent classical answers. The parameterized generator constructs gates without an arithmetic lookup table or a dense unitary matrix. Logical scaling is measured separately from the bounded simulations. One fixed-base surface-code projection is computed using the audited QDK mean synthesis-cost model; it is not a certified Clifford+T circuit or a general factoring benchmark.

Given N and a chosen base a with \gcd(a,N)=1, the order is the smallest positive r satisfying a^r\equiv1\pmod N. If a verified period is even, let b=a^{r/2}\bmod N. Nontrivial values of \gcd(b-1,N) and \gcd(b+1,N) give factors. Odd periods and b=\pm1 can fail, so they must not disappear from success accounting.

Our input is the classical pair (N,a). It specifies ordinary gate constants and the bit width n=\lceil\log_2N\rceil; there is no external database or amplitude-loading oracle. The work register begins at 1, while the t exponent qubits begin in a uniform superposition. Controlled multiplication by a^{2^j}\bmod N entangles the jth exponent bit with the modular-power register. All work ancillas are uncomputed before the inverse QFT and exponent readout.

The arithmetic follows Fourier addition and compute–swap–uncompute multiplication 

Draper, 2000

Beauregard, 2003, using an original Qiskit 2.6.2 implementation. Qiskit is Apache-2.0 software; see its 

upstream repository and our 

MIT implementation.

For 0\le y<N, a modular addition uses an (n+1)-bit accumulator and one borrow flag. In the Fourier basis it adds a constant c, subtracts N, conditionally restores N after inspecting the high bit, and removes the borrow information using the relation between the result and c. QFTs, controlled phase gates, X gates and CX gates implement every step. Addition by c is controlled; the subtract/restore work cancels on inactive control branches. The accumulator’s high bit and borrow flag return to zero.

To multiply by a, add a2^j\bmod N into a zero accumulator, controlled by each input bit. Swap the input with the result under the exponent control. Then subtract the binary-weighted multiples of a^{-1}\bmod N controlled by the new input bits. The old input is erased because a^{-1}(ax\bmod N)\equiv x\pmod N. This includes the inverse arithmetic, rather than charging an opaque modular-multiplication box.

The contract requires x<N, a zero accumulator and a clean flag. Outside that subspace the same gate circuit remains reversible, but we assign it no modular-arithmetic meaning. All QFT angles are numerical representations of exact analytic angles; fault-tolerant synthesis is a separate layer.

In-memory arithmetic preserves the relative phases needed for coherent controls. The pinned QASM exporter omits the compiled circuit’s overall global phase, recorded in the ledger. Our QASM files describe complete measured trials with unchanged probabilities; they are not specifications for a phase-preserving oracle to be coherently controlled again.

The first example is N=15,a=2,t=4. Its 14-wire circuit includes four exponent bits, four modular-power bits, a five-bit accumulator and one borrow flag. In the figure, cM2 and cM4 are controlled multiplication by two and four modulo 15. Modular exponentiation computes each circuit constant without computing the order. Constants that equal one produce identity multipliers and are omitted; the favorable order of this tiny instance is disclosed in the scaling table.

Continued fractions reconstruct a denominator from y/2^t. Modular exponentiation verifies each candidate, then the gcd factors are checked. A verified denominator is a period and can be a multiple of the minimal order at finite precision; no hidden order enumeration or candidate trial division is used. Here y=4,12 give period four and factors 3,5; y=0,8 fail. Thus the ideal fixed-base factor probability is 1/2 per full trial. Eight independent complete trials make ideal sampling failure at most 1/256<0.005. The notebook executes eight seeded draws from the validated circuit distribution and shows every outcome, including failures.

For N=21,a=2,t=6, the order is six and does not divide the 64-point Fourier grid. The actual 18-wire circuit is checked against the finite Fourier sum, not an assumption of exact peaks. With the same reconstruction rule, ideal factor success is about 0.287989, requiring 16 full trials for ideal sampling failure at most 0.005. logical wires. There are at most t nonidentity controlled multipliers, each with 2n modular additions and n controlled swaps. Exact QFT addition costs O(n^2) elementary operations, so this implementation has O(tn^3+t^2) gates, or O(n^4) for t=2n. This deliberately transparent arithmetic is not an optimized factoring resource benchmark. The 

measured scaling CSV gives actual expanded counts for N=7,15,21,33 with t=2n; these larger materializations are not claimed simulated. Instance-specific identity powers affect the observed counts.

With t=2n, the grid spacing is at most 1/N^2. A closest sample to a phase s/r is then fine enough for continued-fraction reconstruction; recovery of r still requires an appropriate numerator, and factoring can still fail after a valid period. For a fixed instance with independently established ideal success p, R=\lceil\log\delta_{\rm sample}/\log(1-p)\rceil complete trials give the ideal retry bound. Total logical work is R times the complete trial count. The measured toy values of p must not be extrapolated to arbitrary integers.

The N=15,t=4 export contains 8,665 unitary primitives and four exponent measurements per full trial. Its dependency depth is a compiler graph property, not physical runtime. Preparation, all arithmetic and uncomputation, inverse QFT and readout are included. The eight-trial contract charges 69,352 primitive operations including readout. Classical constant construction, continued fractions, modular exponentiation and gcd verification run on the classical processor; generated metadata records measured construction/compilation and seeded postprocessing timings, separately from physical projections. Their classical bit-complexity is polynomial using ordinary modular arithmetic. The enumerated order reference is bounded validation work and is not part of the algorithm.

This is fixed-base success accounting. A general factoring driver also needs classical preliminary checks, random-base choices, noncoprime-base gcd successes, unfavorable periods, phase-precision selection and their combined success bound. Those parts are not projected by this report.

The 

computed surface-code report imports the entire measured circuit into QDK 1.34.0 and models eight serial executions. It uses the illustrative frozen hardware profile p=10^{-4}, 100 ns gate time and 500 ns measurement time, a separate 0.005 physical-fault allowance over all eight trials, and a 10-5 synthesis-model allowance per trial. The independent ideal sampling allowance is also 0.005. These distinct quantities do not establish a certified combined factoring confidence.

QDK’s canonical trace has 2,737 arbitrary rotations, 1,599 exact T instructions and four measurements. Its mean-fit allocation is 20 T states per arbitrary rotation, totaling 56,339 T states per execution. The modeled synthesis scalar is about 6.89\times10^{-6} per trial. It supplies neither a concrete synthesis sequence nor a per-angle approximation certificate. The QDK layout also abstracts Clifford scheduling.

An explicit diagonal two-qubit Gibbs purification and its reduced thermal state are checked against an independent normalized matrix exponential. A thermal mixed state favors low-energy configurations without selecting one ground state. A purification stores those probabilities as amplitudes entangled with a reference; tracing out the reference gives the mixed state. Noncommuting Hamiltonians require an actual quantum filter or other preparation procedure rather than direct classical basis weights.

For a stated finite Hamiltonian and inverse temperature \beta in inverse energy units, the thermal target is\rho_\beta=\frac{e^{-\beta H}}{Z_\beta},\qquad Z_\beta=\operatorname{Tr}(e^{-\beta H}).

This page distinguishes that density operator, its purification, and measured thermal observables. Algorithmic Gibbs preparation requires access, normalization and spectral assumptions; the original preparation methods provide context 

Poulin & Wocjan, 2009. Our first circuit instead uses an explicitly enumerated diagonal model and pays its classical coefficient-loading cost.

UseH/E_0=0.6Z_0Z_1+0.35Z_0-0.2Z_1,\qquad E_0=1,\qquad k_B=1.

The coefficients are expressed in the chosen energy unit E_0=1. At \beta=1.25/E_0, temperature is T=0.8E_0. The Hamiltonian is diagonal in the computational basis, with no unknown eigenbasis or diagonalization step. In displayed bit order q1 q0, the energies of 00, 01, 10, 11 are (0.75,-1.15,-0.05,0.45)E_0. Every system and reference wire starts in zero.

We compute all energies, shifted Boltzmann weights and rotation angles classically. With E_{\min} as a stability shift,p_x=\frac{e^{-\beta(E_x-E_{\min})}}{\sum_y e^{-\beta(E_y-E_{\min})}},\qquad
\log Z_\beta=-\beta E_{\min}+\log\sum_y e^{-\beta(E_y-E_{\min})}.

The shift preserves the state but its contribution to normalization is recorded. At the default temperature, probabilities are approximately (0.0627972,0.6751331,0.1707004,0.0913693) and \log Z=1.8303454. Exhaustive energy enumeration takes O(n2^n) operations and O(2^n) storage; the loader is not a scalable Gibbs algorithm.

The original generator uses a binary tree of conditional probability masses. At each prefix it applies an explicit controlled R_Y rotation with angle 2\operatorname{atan2}(\sqrt{p_{\rm right}},\sqrt{p_{\rm left}}), preparing\sum_x\sqrt{p_x}|x\rangle_S.

System-to-reference CX gates then produce|\Psi_\beta\rangle=\sum_x\sqrt{p_x}|x\rangle_S|x\rangle_R,\qquad
\operatorname{Tr}_R|\Psi_\beta\rangle\langle\Psi_\beta|=\rho_\beta.

Controlled-rotation state loading is a standard constructive approach 

Möttönen et al., 2005; the code here is original. It contains explicit gates rather than an opaque state-preparation or dense-unitary operation. System wires are q0,q1 and reference wires q2,q3.

An ideal circuit specifies logical operations. A physical processor must implement them while qubits, gates, measurements, and idle periods can fail. Fault tolerance encodes information across many physical qubits and repeatedly measures error syndromes. These measurements reveal information about errors while preserving the encoded quantum information. The result is a logical operation with a modeled failure probability and a physical space and time cost.

The surface code uses local stabilizer checks on a two-dimensional layout. Its code distance characterizes the smallest undetectable logical error. Increasing distance consumes more physical qubits and more syndrome rounds; the required distance depends on the noise model, decoder, and permitted failure probability. A threshold is a property of those assumptions, rather than a guarantee supplied by the algorithm’s logical qubit count. 

Fowler and colleagues’ surface-code review introduces these constructions and their implementation costs.

Layout matters. Logical data patches, routing space, temporary ancillas, and measurement procedures contribute to the footprint. Operations performed through lattice surgery occupy patches for several syndrome rounds. A logical circuit’s abstract gate depth therefore needs a timing and scheduling model before it becomes elapsed physical time.

Clifford operations preserve stabilizer structure. Universal computation also needs non-Clifford operations, commonly T gates or equivalent injected resources. A factory distills noisy resource states into states suitable for logical computation. Its footprint, throughput, output error, and number of parallel copies must be included in the report. The mathematical task is to connect a problem specification to a circuit and a checkable output. This primer collects notation used by the algorithm chapters. It complements the 

quantum-physics primer; no background in formal proof software is required.

A ket |v\rangle is a complex column vector; its bra \langle v| is the conjugate transpose. The inner product and Euclidean norm are\langle v|w\rangle=\sum_j\overline{v_j}w_j,
\qquad \|v\|_2=\sqrt{\langle v|v\rangle}.

Orthogonal vectors have zero inner product. An orthonormal basis gives coordinates without changing lengths. Normalized state vectors have unit norm, while input data vectors may require a separate normalization factor. 

IBM’s inner-products lesson develops these conventions.

Two registers combine by a tensor product: |v\rangle\otimes|w\rangle. Dimensions multiply, so n qubits have 2^n basis states. A joint vector need not factor into individual-register vectors; this is the mathematical possibility behind entanglement. Register order and bit order must match the generator, simulator, and classical comparison. A statevector containing every amplitude therefore has very different storage requirements from a circuit description.

Matrices act linearly on vectors. The adjoint A^\dagger conjugates and transposes; a unitary satisfies U^\dagger U=I and preserves inner products. A Hermitian matrix satisfies H^\dagger=H and has real eigenvalues with an orthonormal eigenbasis:H|u_j\rangle=\lambda_j|u_j\rangle,\qquad
H=\sum_j\lambda_j|u_j\rangle\langle u_j|.

Phase estimation targets the phase in U|u_j\rangle=e^{2\pi i\phi_j}|u_j\rangle. The prepared state’s overlap with the relevant eigenvector affects the chance of obtaining that phase.

Watch Gilbert Strang’s 

MIT 18.06 video, “Lecture 21: Eigenvalues and eigenvectors” for the underlying eigenvector equation. The official lesson includes a video and transcript; quantum phase estimation applies this idea to unitary operators.

A norm makes “close” quantitative. The operator norm\|A\|=\sup_{\|v\|_2=1}\|Av\|_2

measures the largest amplification of a vector. The trace norm \|A\|_1 is the sum of singular values, and the Frobenius norm \|A\|_F=\sqrt{\operatorname{Tr}(A^\dagger A)} measures all entries together. These norms give different error guarantees.

For Hermitian H, define f(H) by applying f to its eigenvalues. If a polynomial p approximates f uniformly on an interval containing the spectrum, then\sup_{x\in[a,b]}|p(x)-f(x)|\leq\epsilon
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\|p(H)-f(H)\|\leq\epsilon.

This motivates polynomial methods for evolution and inversion. QSP/QSVT circuits also impose encoding, boundedness, and parity conditions; an arbitrary polynomial fit alone is insufficient. 

PennyLane’s QSVT introduction explains this connection.

Linear-system algorithms must additionally track conditioning. For an invertible matrix, the spectral condition number is \kappa=\sigma_{\max}/\sigma_{\min}. Small singular values can make inversion sensitive and expensive. Producing a state proportional to A^{-1}b also leaves its normalization and requested readout to be accounted for. It does not directly return a classical list of every solution component.

For independent preparations with success probability p, R trials all fail with probability (1-p)^R. Repetition costs belong in the algorithm estimate.

For independent Bernoulli outcomes X_1,\ldots,X_M with common mean p, the frequency \hat p=M^{-1}\sum_iX_i estimates that probability. Hoeffding’s bound gives\Pr(|\hat p-p|\geq\epsilon)\leq2e^{-2M\epsilon^2}.

Thus M\geq\ln(2/\delta)/(2\epsilon^2) suffices for confidence at least 1-\delta. 

John Duchi’s Stanford notes state the independence and boundedness assumptions. Sampling confidence controls random variation; it does not remove a biased circuit or an inaccurate model. Specify those errors separately when comparing quantum and classical outputs.

Quantum algorithms use quantum physics to transform information and extract a specified result. This appendix introduces the finite-dimensional language used throughout the handbook. Read it alongside the 

mathematics primer, then follow the quantities you actually need to reproduce an algorithm.

A pure state is a normalized complex vector |\psi\rangle. For one qubit,|\psi\rangle=\alpha|0\rangle+\beta|1\rangle,
\qquad |\alpha|^2+|\beta|^2=1.

Relative phases affect interference. Multiplying the whole vector by the same phase leaves its physical state unchanged. A state describes the system; an observable describes a measurable quantity. Observables are Hermitian operators, such as the Pauli Z operator or the Hamiltonian H, which represents energy.

A density matrix also describes mixtures and subsystems entangled with an environment:\rho=\sum_j p_j|\psi_j\rangle\langle\psi_j|,
\qquad p_j\geq0,\quad \sum_jp_j=1.

It is positive semidefinite and has trace one. Pure states have \rho=|\psi\rangle\langle\psi|; different ensembles can describe the same mixed state. Ignoring part of a joint system gives its reduced density matrix by a partial trace. 

IBM’s density-matrix lesson develops this broader description.

For example, |+\rangle=(|0\rangle+|1\rangle)/\sqrt2 and the mixture \rho=I/2 both give equal computational-basis probabilities. They differ when measured in the X basis: the pure state always gives the +1 outcome, whereas the mixture gives either outcome equally often. Matching one measurement distribution therefore does not establish that two states agree.

For an observable A=\sum_a aP_a, a projective measurement returns eigenvalue a with Born-rule probabilityp(a)=\operatorname{Tr}(P_a\rho),
\qquad \langle A\rangle=\operatorname{Tr}(A\rho).

The projectors P_a include any degeneracy. Measuring a pure state in the computational basis gives p(x)=|\langle x|\psi\rangle|^2. One shot produces an outcome; estimating an expectation generally requires repeated preparations and measurements.

For the physical connection between eigenvectors and measurement, watch Barton Zwiebach’s 

MIT 8.04 video, “Completeness of eigenvectors and measurement postulate”. Its official lesson page includes the video and transcript.

Closed-system evolution is unitary:\rho(t)=U(t)\rho(0)U(t)^\dagger,\qquad
U(t)=e^{-iHt/\hbar}

for a time-independent Hamiltonian. Circuit gates approximate or compose such transformations; the simulation chapters usually set \hbar=1.

Noise, discarded ancillas, and measurements averaged over their outcomes require quantum channels. A completely positive, trace-preserving map has a Kraus representation\mathcal E(\rho)=\sum_jK_j\rho K_j^\dagger,
\qquad \sum_jK_j^\dagger K_j=I.

Complete positivity ensures valid states even when the input is entangled with another system. Trace preservation retains total probability. A selected measurement branch can instead decrease the trace; that trace records the branch’s success probability. 

IBM’s channel representations explain the channel viewpoint and its implementations.

For a finite-dimensional Hamiltonian, the Gibbs state at inverse temperature \beta=1/(k_BT) is\rho_\beta=\frac{e^{-\beta H}}{Z(\beta)},
\qquad Z(\beta)=\operatorname{Tr}(e^{-\beta H}).

The partition function normalizes the state; exponentiating a Hamiltonian alone does not produce a normalized density matrix. Energy eigenstates receive weights proportional to e^{-\beta E_j}. See David Tong’s 

statistical-physics notes on the canonical ensemble.

Choose an output metric before estimating resources. A search task needs a correct answer with stated probability. An energy task needs observable accuracy and sampling confidence. A state-preparation task may use trace distance D(\rho,\sigma)=\tfrac12\|\rho-\sigma\|_1, which bounds changes in measurement-event probabilities. Fidelity measures similarity; specify whether it is squared or unsquared, as 

IBM’s fidelity lesson emphasizes. The 

resource baseline accounts separately for algorithmic approximation, sampling requirements, and physical faults.

Run the following cells in Binder or a local JupyterLab kernel to use Python controls. The published book shows saved circuit and probability outputs; its separate browser explorer computes the ideal probability formula.

The notebook controls regenerate the actual Qiskit circuit and exact statevector for 2–6 qubits and 0–12 Grover iterations. The marked value adapts to the register size. Every evaluation checks the simulated marked-state probability against the analytic formula.

import os
import numpy as np


def simulate_interactive_case(n_qubits, marked, iterations):
    """Bounded ideal simulation shared by the controls and deterministic checks."""
    if not 2 <= n_qubits <= 6:
        raise ValueError("Live controls support 2–6 qubits")
    if not 0 <= iterations <= 12:
        raise ValueError("Live controls support 0–12 iterations")
    marked = min(max(int(marked), 0), 2**n_qubits - 1)
    circuit = build_grover_circuit(n_qubits, marked, iterations)
    probabilities = Statevector.from_instruction(circuit).probabilities()
    expected = expected_success_probability(n_qubits, iterations)
    np.testing.assert_allclose(probabilities[marked], expected, atol=1e-10, rtol=0)
    return circuit, probabilities, marked, expected


for validation_n in range(2, 7):
    for validation_marked in (0, 2**validation_n - 1):
        for validation_iterations in (0, optimal_iterations(validation_n), 12):
            simulate_interactive_case(validation_n, validation_marked, validation_iterations)
print("Validated 30 bounded cases; every live evaluation also checks the analytic probability.")




# The book build skips widget creation so it never publishes inert controls.
# Binder and local kernels display live controls when this cell is run.
if os.environ.get("OPENQUANTUM_STATIC_BUILD") == "1":
    print("Live Python controls are available when this notebook is run in Binder or JupyterLab.")
else:
    import ipywidgets as widgets
    from IPython.display import display

    n_control = widgets.IntSlider(value=3, min=2, max=6, description="Qubits", continuous_update=False)
    marked_control = widgets.IntSlider(value=5, min=0, max=7, description="Marked", continuous_update=False)
    iterations_control = widgets.IntSlider(value=2, min=0, max=12, description="Iterations", continuous_update=False)

    def update_marked_range(change):
        marked_control.max = 2**change["new"] - 1
        marked_control.value = min(marked_control.value, marked_control.max)

    n_control.observe(update_marked_range, names="value")

    def render_live_case(n_qubits, marked, iterations):
        circuit, probabilities, marked, expected = simulate_interactive_case(n_qubits, marked, iterations)
        target = f"{marked:0{n_qubits}b}"
        print(f"Target {target}; {iterations} iterations; first-peak choice {optimal_iterations(n_qubits)}")
        print(f"Statevector probability {probabilities[marked]:.10f}; analytic probability {expected:.10f}")
        print("Ideal circuit: no device noise or fault-tolerant resource model is applied here.")
        circuit_figure = circuit.draw(output="mpl", fold=32, scale=0.65)
        display(circuit_figure)
        plt.close(circuit_figure)
        figure, axis = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3.2))
        indices = list(range(len(probabilities)))
        labels = [f"{i:0{n_qubits}b}" for i in indices]
        axis.bar(indices, probabilities, color=["#1c766c" if i == marked else "#b5c6d2" for i in indices])
        ticks = indices if n_qubits <= 4 else sorted({0, marked, len(probabilities) - 1})
        axis.set_xticks(ticks, [labels[i] for i in ticks])
        axis.set(xlabel="Bitstring (most significant bit first)", ylabel="Ideal measurement probability", ylim=(0, 1))
        figure.tight_layout()
        display(figure)
        plt.close(figure)

    live_output = widgets.interactive_output(render_live_case, {
        "n_qubits": n_control, "marked": marked_control, "iterations": iterations_control
    })
    display(widgets.VBox([widgets.HBox([n_control, marked_control, iterations_control]), live_output]))

The degree-4 polynomial is classically aggregated in the Pauli basis with a strict term cap. Its PREPARE uses controlled RY rotations, SELECT uses indexed Pauli operations and coefficient phases, and inverse PREPARE is present. This bounded preprocessing is not a scalable word-indexed Taylor oracle. All label outcomes must be zero. No amplitude-amplification circuit is implemented.

lcu_rows = []
for segments in (1, 2, 4, 8):
    access = lcu.build_taylor_lcu(terms, 1 / segments, 4)
    conditional, success, per_segment = lcu.postselected_lcu_evolution(access, initial, segments)
    value = float(np.vdot(conditional, Z0 @ conditional).real)
    lcu_rows.append({"segments": segments, "terms": len(access.terms), "normalization": access.normalization,
                     "conditional_state_error": float(np.linalg.norm(conditional - exact @ initial)),
                     "observable_error": abs(value - exact_z), "whole_attempt_success": success,
                     "attempts_for_one_measured_trial_99_percent": lcu.postselection_attempts(success, .01)})
display(pd.DataFrame(lcu_rows))



The state-error checks above describe the conditional state before final system readout. The exported attempt measures every system wire, so its retry bound obtains one accepted measured trial with at least 99% ideal acceptance probability. Estimating an observable needs many accepted measured trials and a new whole-workload retry/confidence budget. records.content:
The MaxCut graph is the cycle with vertices 0,1,2,3 and edges (0,1),(1,2),(2,3),(0,3). The objective is the number of cut edges,C(z)=\sum_{(u,v)}\frac{1-Z_uZ_v}{2}.

Qiskit wire q[0] is the least significant bit. Displayed bitstrings read q[3] q[2] q[1] q[0]. We enumerate all 16 assignments before using a quantum circuit.

For VQE the input is the explicit HamiltonianH=-Z_0-Z_1+\tfrac12X_0X_1.

The independent NumPy matrix uses basis order |00\rangle,|01\rangle,|10\rangle,|11\rangle. Exact diagonalization is a reference calculation on this four-dimensional input.

edges = tuple(opt.CYCLE_EDGES)
n_qubits = 4
cut_values = np.array([
    sum(((assignment >> u) & 1) != ((assignment >> v) & 1) for u, v in edges)
    for assignment in range(2**n_qubits)
], dtype=float)
np.testing.assert_array_equal(opt.maxcut_values(n_qubits, edges), cut_values)
classical_cut_optimum = float(cut_values.max())
classical_best_strings = [f"{i:04b}" for i in np.flatnonzero(cut_values == classical_cut_optimum)]

I = np.eye(2)
X = np.array([[0., 1.], [1., 0.]])
Z = np.diag([1., -1.])
independent_hamiltonian = -np.kron(I, Z) - np.kron(Z, I) + .5*np.kron(X, X)
np.testing.assert_allclose(opt.vqe_hamiltonian(), independent_hamiltonian, atol=1e-14, rtol=0)
exact_eigenvalues = np.linalg.eigvalsh(independent_hamiltonian)
exact_ground_energy = float(exact_eigenvalues[0])
np.testing.assert_allclose(exact_ground_energy, -np.sqrt(4.25), atol=1e-14, rtol=0)
print({"MaxCut optimum": classical_cut_optimum, "optimal bitstrings": classical_best_strings,
       "Hamiltonian eigenvalues": exact_eigenvalues.tolist()})

records.content:
Depth-one QAOA prepares |+\rangle^{\otimes4}, applies e^{-i\gamma C}, then e^{-i\beta\sum_jX_j}. Each cost edge is implemented by CX; RZ(-gamma); CX; its omitted global phase does not affect the output. The mixer uses RX(2 beta). The minimizer receives -\langle C\rangle.

The VQE circuit prepares R_Y(\theta) on qubit 0 and then CX(0,1). It has state \cos(\theta/2)|00\rangle+\sin(\theta/2)|11\rangle and minimizes \langle H\rangle.

Every objective evaluation below checks the independently derived formulas\langle C\rangle=2+\sin(4\beta)\sin(2\gamma),\qquad
E(\theta)=-2\cos\theta+\tfrac12\sin\theta.

The deterministic coordinate polling optimizer starts with step 0.4 radians, evaluates both directions of each coordinate in a fixed order, accepts an improvement greater than 

10-12, and halves its step when no candidate improves the current value. It stops when the step is below 

10-6 radians or after 128 iterations. Angles are periodic modulo 2\pi. These stopping rules are empirical search settings, not a bound on the objective gap.

All three initializations are fixed below. The first run is selected for plots and sampled readout in advance. The complete canonical traces, including every trial objective and measured optimizer time, are in the downloadable runs.json and evaluations.csv. This notebook executes new reproductions; its measured times can differ from those artifacts.

def checked_qaoa_objective(parameters):
    gamma, beta = parameters
    observed = opt.qaoa_expectation(n_qubits, edges, [gamma], [beta])
    predicted = 2 + np.sin(4*beta)*np.sin(2*gamma)
    np.testing.assert_allclose(observed, predicted, atol=2e-12, rtol=0)
    return -observed


def checked_vqe_objective(parameters):
    theta = parameters[0]
    observed = opt.vqe_expectation(theta)
    predicted = -2*np.cos(theta) + .5*np.sin(theta)
    np.testing.assert_allclose(observed, predicted, atol=2e-12, rtol=0)
    return observed


search_settings = dict(initial_step=.4, step_tolerance=1e-6,
                       improvement_tolerance=1e-12, max_iterations=128)
qaoa_initializations = [(0.2, 0.1), (0.6, 0.4), (-0.3, 0.25)]
vqe_initializations = [(0.6,), (-1.1,), (2.2,)]
qaoa_runs, vqe_runs = [], []
reproduction_seconds = {"qaoa": [], "vqe": []}
for name, objective, starts, destination in (
    ("qaoa", checked_qaoa_objective, qaoa_initializations, qaoa_runs),
    ("vqe", checked_vqe_objective, vqe_initializations, vqe_runs),
):
    for initial in starts:
        started = perf_counter()
        result = opt.pattern_search(objective, initial, objective_method="exact_statevector", **search_settings)
        reproduction_seconds[name].append(perf_counter() - started)
        destination.append(result)

qaoa_result, vqe_result = qaoa_runs[0], vqe_runs[0]
gamma, beta = qaoa_result["parameters"]
theta = vqe_result["parameters"][0]
qaoa_expected_cut = -qaoa_result["value"]
vqe_energy = vqe_result["value"]
assert abs(qaoa_expected_cut - 3) < 1e-8
assert abs(vqe_energy - exact_ground_energy) < 1e-8
print("All objective evaluations passed their independent analytic checks.")



rows = ["| Workflow / fixed start | Final exact objective | Evaluations | Iterations | Stop | Reproduction seconds |",
        "|---|---:|---:|---:|---|---:|"]
for name, starts, runs in (("QAOA expected cut", qaoa_initializations, qaoa_runs),
                          ("VQE energy", vqe_initializations, vqe_runs)):
    for index, (initial, result) in enumerate(zip(starts, runs)):
        objective = -result["value"] if name.startswith("QAOA") else result["value"]
        seconds = reproduction_seconds["qaoa" if name.startswith("QAOA") else "vqe"][index]
        rows.append(f"| {name}, {initial} | {objective:.10f} | {len(result['evaluations'])} | "
                    f"{len(result['iterations'])} | {result['stop_reason']} | {seconds:.4f} |")
rows += ["", f"The classical cut optimum is {classical_cut_optimum:g}; the first QAOA run's exact expected-cut ratio is "
         f"{qaoa_expected_cut/classical_cut_optimum:.10f}. The first VQE run's gap to the exact ground energy is "
         f"{vqe_energy-exact_ground_energy:.3g}. These are exact-statevector results on the specified small inputs."]

colors = ["#246b72", "#a2573c", "#7a6a9b"]
for run, color, initial in zip(qaoa_runs, colors, qaoa_initializations):
    values = np.array([entry["value"] for entry in run["evaluations"]])
    axes[0].plot(np.arange(1, len(values)+1), -np.minimum.accumulate(values),
                 color=color, label=str(initial))
axes[0].axhline(3, color="#555555", ls="--", lw=1, label="depth-one optimum")

            title="QAOA: prescribed initializations")

records.content:
Optimization above uses zero shots: each objective is evaluated by an ideal statevector. The following held-out sampling experiments evaluate the first optimized parameters with seeds 7, 19 and 41. They do not train a noisy or sampled optimizer.

For QAOA, a single all-Z measurement of all four qubits supplies every edge contribution and a candidate cut. Each seeded experiment uses 2,048 independently simulated shots.

For VQE, measure both qubits in Z to estimate the joint observable -Z_0-Z_1, preserving the covariance of its terms. In a separate group, apply H to both qubits and measure Z to estimate \tfrac12X_0X_1. Each group uses 2,048 shots per seed. Group sample means are added, and their sample variances determine a descriptive estimated standard error. This standard error is not a confidence or device-error guarantee.

Sampling uses the implementation’s NumPy Generator(PCG64) multinomial sampler from the actual circuit probabilities. The QAOA and VQE Z groups use the listed seed; the independent VQE X stream uses that seed plus 1,000,003. The notebook recomputes every sampled mean and group standard error directly from the returned counts. State preparation and the change of measurement basis are present in the generated circuits. Device noise, mitigation, fault-tolerant synthesis and hardware execution time are excluded.

shots_per_group = 2048
sampling_seeds = (7, 19, 41)
z_group_probabilities = Statevector.from_instruction(opt.build_vqe_circuit(theta, basis="z")).probabilities()
x_group_probabilities = Statevector.from_instruction(opt.build_vqe_circuit(theta, basis="x")).probabilities()
indices_two = np.arange(4)
z0 = 1-2*(indices_two & 1)
z1 = 1-2*((indices_two >> 1) & 1)
z_group_values = -z0-z1
x_group_values = .5*z0*z1
np.testing.assert_allclose(np.dot(z_group_probabilities, z_group_values)
                           + np.dot(x_group_probabilities, x_group_values),
                           vqe_energy, atol=1e-12, rtol=0)


def observed_mean_and_standard_error(counts_by_bitstring, values):
    counts = np.array([counts_by_bitstring.get(f"{index:0{int(np.log2(len(values)))}b}", 0)
                       for index in range(len(values))])
    count = int(np.sum(counts))
    mean = float(np.dot(counts, values)/count)
    variance = float(np.dot(counts, (values-mean)**2)/(count-1))
    return mean, np.sqrt(variance/count)


sample_records = []
for seed in sampling_seeds:
    q_readout = opt.sample_qaoa(gamma, beta, shots=shots_per_group, seed=seed)
    v_readout = opt.sample_vqe(theta, shots=shots_per_group, seed=seed)
    q_mean, q_se = observed_mean_and_standard_error(q_readout["counts"], cut_values)
    z_group, x_group = v_readout["groups"]
    z_mean, z_se = observed_mean_and_standard_error(z_group["counts"], z_group_values)
    x_mean, x_se = observed_mean_and_standard_error(x_group["counts"], x_group_values)
    np.testing.assert_allclose([q_mean, q_se],
                               [q_readout["estimate"], q_readout["estimated_standard_error"]],
                               atol=1e-12, rtol=0)
    np.testing.assert_allclose([z_mean+x_mean, np.hypot(z_se, x_se)],
                               [v_readout["estimate"], v_readout["estimated_standard_error"]],
                               atol=1e-12, rtol=0)
    assert sum(q_readout["counts"].values()) == shots_per_group
    assert sum(z_group["counts"].values()) == shots_per_group
    assert sum(x_group["counts"].values()) == shots_per_group
    sample_records.append({"seed": seed, "qaoa": q_readout, "vqe": v_readout})
rows = ["| Seed | Sampled mean cut | Cut SE | Optimal-cut fraction | Sampled VQE energy | Energy SE |",
        "|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|"]
for record in sample_records:
    q, v = record["qaoa"], record["vqe"]
    rows.append(f"| {record['seed']} | {q['estimate']:.6f} | {q['estimated_standard_error']:.6f} | "
                f"{q['optimal_cut_sample_fraction']:.6f} | {v['estimate']:.6f} | {v['estimated_standard_error']:.6f} |")
display_result_table(rows)
print({"exact-optimization shots": 0, "sampled QAOA shots across three seeds": 3*shots_per_group,
       "sampled VQE shots across three seeds and two groups": 3*2*shots_per_group,
       "combined sampled shots": 3*3*shots_per_group})

This notebook applies the previous finite-shot schedule to a three-vertex triangle and a second two-qubit Hamiltonian. The circuit family, shot schedule, acceptance margin and stopping rule are fixed. We do not retune them after observing these results.

Each task starts at the same parameters across seeds 7, 19, and 41: QAOA starts at (gamma,beta)=(0.2,0.1), and VQE at theta=0.6. Varying the seed now isolates seeded sampling variation in this ideal model rather than jointly changing the initial point. Three seeds remain a small teaching check, not a distributional performance guarantee.

Independent ideal measurements are simulated by drawing counts from explicit circuit statevector probabilities. Measured outcomes and their descriptive standard errors drive every parameter decision. Exact values are computed only afterward to audit quality and display the trajectories. Failed targets remain visible.

Use the pinned Python 3.12 environment. The notebook loads its worktree source explicitly or a matching portability optimization.py download placed beside it. Saved outputs serve a static site without a live kernel. QAOA and VQE follow the original algorithm papers

records.content:
The triangle has edges (0,1),(1,2),(0,2). The task maximizes C(z)=\sum_{(u,v)}[z_u\ne z_v], and training minimizes the negative sampled cut mean. Enumerating all eight assignments gives maximum cut two. Bitstrings read q_2q_1q_0.

QAOA prepares |+\rangle^{\otimes3} with H on all three qubits. It uses CX–RZ(−\gamma)–CX on each edge and RX(2\beta) on every qubit. Angles are radians with R_P(\alpha)=e^{-i\alpha P/2}. A single all-Z group scores all three edges jointly. The cycle’s earlier scalar energy formula does not apply to this graph; below we independently apply the diagonal cost phase and an explicit NumPy tensor-product mixer.

For VQE, the new dimensionless Hamiltonian isH=-0.8Z_0-0.6Z_1+0.4X_0X_1.

The ansatz still prepares |00\rangle, applies RY(\theta) on qubit zero, then CX(0,1). One joint all-Z group scores -0.8Z_0-0.6Z_1, retaining covariance; the all-X group scores 0.4X_0X_1 after H basis changes on both qubits. Every shot needs a fresh preparation.

The post-run reference ground energy is -\sqrt{2.12}. The ansatz expectation is E(\theta)=-1.4\cos\theta+0.4\sin\theta. Full matrix diagonalization below checks the reference rather than assuming that the ansatz subspace contains the global minimum.

The initial objective uses 256 shots per group. Each of 32 sweeps freshly measures the incumbent and all negative and positive coordinate proposals, then accepts the best proposal only if its sampled decrease exceeds twice the combined estimated standard error. The four eight-sweep blocks remain:

The rule is a fixed-budget heuristic, not a calibrated significance test or a convergence certificate. After the schedule ends, each final state receives fresh validation with 4,096 shots per group. Validation and exact audits do not choose training moves.

The predeclared post-run targets are expected triangle cut at least 1.90 and exact VQE energy gap at most 0.03 above -\sqrt{2.12}. These refer to exact post-run quality, not uncertainty on the sampled estimate. All seeds retain the same initial point per task. Algorithm IDs 2 and 3 distinguish the new tasks from earlier random streams; PCG64 uses SeedSequence([seed, algorithm_id], spawn_key=(family, call_index, group_index)), with family zero for training and one for validation. Stream separation supports reproducibility; pseudorandom keys do not themselves prove the independent-sampling model.

# The same finite-shot settings run on two new explicitly stated inputs.
portable = opt.run_portability_demo()
assert portable["exact_diagnostics_used_for_optimization"] is False
assert portable["physical_resource_estimate"] is None
for algorithm, initial in (("qaoa", [.2, .1]), ("vqe", [.6])):
    assert [run["seed"] for run in portable[algorithm]["runs"]] == [7, 19, 41]
    for run in portable[algorithm]["runs"]:
        np.testing.assert_allclose(run["initial"], initial, rtol=0, atol=1e-14)
print({"new_instance_seed_cases": sum(len(portable[a]["runs"]) for a in ("qaoa", "vqe")),
       "training_modeled_shots": portable["training_shots"],
       "fresh_validation_modeled_shots": portable["validation_shots"],
       "total_modeled_shots": portable["total_shots"],
       "workflow_CPU_wall_seconds": portable["workflow_wall_seconds"]})




edges = ((0, 1), (1, 2), (0, 2))
n_qubits = 3
cut_values = np.array([sum(((z >> u) & 1) != ((z >> v) & 1) for u, v in edges)
                       for z in range(1 << n_qubits)], dtype=float)
np.testing.assert_array_equal(cut_values, opt.maxcut_values(n_qubits, edges))
assert cut_values.max() == 2
I = np.eye(2)
X = np.array([[0., 1.], [1., 0.]])
Z = np.diag([1., -1.])
reference_hamiltonian = -.8*np.kron(I, Z) - .6*np.kron(Z, I) + .4*np.kron(X, X)
np.testing.assert_allclose(portable["vqe"]["reference"]["matrix"], reference_hamiltonian, rtol=0, atol=1e-14)
assert {tuple(edge) for edge in portable["qaoa"]["edges"]} == set(edges)
reference_spectrum = np.linalg.eigvalsh(reference_hamiltonian)
reference_energy = float(reference_spectrum[0])
np.testing.assert_allclose(reference_energy, -np.sqrt(2.12), rtol=0, atol=1e-14)


def triangle_reference(parameters):
    gamma, beta = parameters
    # An independent 8-dimensional application of exp(-i gamma C).
    state = np.ones(8, dtype=complex)/np.sqrt(8)
    state *= np.exp(-1j*gamma*cut_values)
    rx = np.cos(beta)*I - 1j*np.sin(beta)*X
    mixer = np.kron(rx, np.kron(rx, rx))
    state = mixer @ state
    return float((np.abs(state)**2) @ cut_values)


# These fixed reference checks are separate from optimizer decisions.
for angles in ((.2, .1), (-.6, .3), (.8, -.2)):
    circuit_state = Statevector.from_instruction(opt.build_qaoa_circuit(n_qubits, edges, [angles[0]], [angles[1]]))
    np.testing.assert_allclose(circuit_state.probabilities() @ cut_values, triangle_reference(angles), rtol=0, atol=1e-12)
print({"triangle_maximum_cut": float(cut_values.max()),
       "maximum_cut_bitstrings": [f"{z:03b}" for z in np.flatnonzero(cut_values == 2)],
       "new_Hamiltonian_spectrum": reference_spectrum.tolist(), "ground_energy": reference_energy})

records.content:
The following check reconstructs every observed mean and sample variance from its measured counts. It then replays the parameter decisions using only measured estimates, standard errors and the prescribed margin. Exact audit fields are excluded from this replay.

All rejected proposals remain in the record and count toward the workload. Re-estimating the incumbent means the displayed sampled trajectory need not be monotone, even when accepted parameter updates appear favorable. The main chapter’s native MyST table is generated independently by the sampled artifact script; this notebook reports its own fresh execution.

def outcome_score(algorithm, group, bits):
    z = int(bits, 2)
    if algorithm == "qaoa":
        return float(sum(((z >> u) & 1) != ((z >> v) & 1) for u, v in edges))
    if group["group"] == "all_z":
        return -.8*(1 - 2*((z >> 0) & 1)) - .6*(1 - 2*((z >> 1) & 1))
    return .4*(1 - 2*((z >> 0) & 1))*(1 - 2*((z >> 1) & 1))


seen_stream_keys = set()
for algorithm in ("qaoa", "vqe"):
    dimension = 2 if algorithm == "qaoa" else 1
    expected_training_calls = 1 + 32*(1 + 2*dimension)
    expected_training_shots = (1 if algorithm == "qaoa" else 2)*(256 + (1 + 2*dimension)*8*(256 + 512 + 1024 + 2048))
    for run in portable[algorithm]["runs"]:
        assert run["objective_evaluations"] == expected_training_calls
        assert run["iteration_count"] == 32
        assert run["stop_reason"] == "fixed_schedule_exhausted"
        assert run["total_shots"] == expected_training_shots
        calls = run["evaluations"]
        for call in calls + [run["validation"]]:
            means, mean_variances = [], []
            for group in call["groups"]:
                assert sum(group["counts"].values()) == group["shots"]
                assert group["rng"]["entropy"] == [run["seed"], 2 if algorithm == "qaoa" else 3]
                stream_key = tuple(group["rng"]["stream_key"])
                assert stream_key not in seen_stream_keys
                seen_stream_keys.add(stream_key)
                mean = sum(count*outcome_score(algorithm, group, bits)
                           for bits, count in group["counts"].items()) / group["shots"]
                variance = sum(count*(outcome_score(algorithm, group, bits) - mean)**2
                               for bits, count in group["counts"].items()) / (group["shots"] - 1)
                np.testing.assert_allclose(mean, group["estimate"], rtol=0, atol=1e-12)
                np.testing.assert_allclose(variance, group["sample_variance"], rtol=1e-12, atol=1e-12)
                means.append(mean)
                mean_variances.append(variance/group["shots"])
            signed_mean = -sum(means) if algorithm == "qaoa" else sum(means)
            np.testing.assert_allclose(signed_mean, call["objective_estimate"], rtol=0, atol=1e-12)
            np.testing.assert_allclose(np.sqrt(sum(mean_variances)), call["estimated_standard_error"], rtol=1e-12, atol=1e-12)
        point = (np.array(run["initial"]) + np.pi) % (2*np.pi) - np.pi
        for iteration in run["iterations"]:
            incumbent = calls[iteration["incumbent_evaluation"]]
            proposals = [calls[index] for index in iteration["proposal_evaluations"]]
            np.testing.assert_allclose(incumbent["parameters"], point, rtol=0, atol=1e-12)
            best = min(proposals, key=lambda item: item["objective_estimate"])
            margin = 2*np.hypot(incumbent["estimated_standard_error"], best["estimated_standard_error"])
            accepted = incumbent["objective_estimate"] - best["objective_estimate"] > margin
            assert accepted == iteration["accepted"]
            assert best["index"] == iteration["best_proposal_evaluation"]
            if accepted:
                point = np.array(best["parameters"])
            np.testing.assert_allclose(iteration["parameters_after"], point, rtol=0, atol=1e-12)
        np.testing.assert_allclose(run["parameters"], point, rtol=0, atol=1e-12)
        assert all(group["rng"]["spawn_key"][0] == 0 for call in calls for group in call["groups"])
        assert all(group["rng"]["spawn_key"][0] == 1 for group in run["validation"]["groups"])
print("Reconstructed all 780 training/validation objective calls from counts and replayed all 192 sampled sweeps.")
